prompt: Where is a method of `Rect` declared in Go?
hint: Look at where `Area` sat in `~/methods`.

choices.text: Inside the braces of `type Rect struct { … }`, after the fields
choices.why: That is where Java and Python put methods. A Go struct's declaration lists fields and nothing else.

choices.text: At package level, as a function with `(r Rect)` before its name
choices.why: Right. The receiver is the extra parameter in front of the name, and the method can sit in any file of the package.

choices.text: In a `class Rect` block that wraps the struct
choices.why: Go has no `class` keyword at all; lesson 1 counted the keywords.

choices.text: In any package that imports `Rect`
choices.why: A method must be declared in the package that defines the type; another package gets `cannot define new methods on non-local type`.

prompt: `type Number = int` is followed by `func (n Number) Triple() int`. What does the compiler say?
hint: What does the `=` make `Number`?

choices.text: Nothing: `Number` is a type of this package, so it may have methods
choices.why: That holds for `type Number int`. With the `=`, `Number` is another name for `int`, which no package of yours defines.

choices.text: `cannot define new methods on non-local type Number`
choices.why: Right. An alias is not a new type, so a method on it is a method on `int`, and that is refused.

choices.text: That a method's receiver must be a struct
choices.why: `Celsius` is a `float64` and has a method; any type the package defines can have them.

choices.text: That `Triple` is already declared on `int`
choices.why: `int` has no methods at all. The refusal is about where the type comes from, not about the name.

prompt: In `func (c Celsius) ToFahrenheit() Fahrenheit`, the `(c Celsius)` written before the method's name is its ___.
hint: It is the value the method is called on.

prompt: `type Span time.Duration` compiles, and then `s.Hours()` on a `Span` is refused. Why?
hint: What does a defined type take from the type it is built on?

choices.text: `Hours` is unexported and cannot be reached from `main`
choices.why: It starts with a capital letter and `time.Duration(s).Hours()` worked from `main`.

choices.text: Methods of `time` types only work on values made by the `time` package
choices.why: Who made the value does not matter. `time.Duration(s)` was made in `main` and had `Hours`.

choices.text: A defined type gets the values and operators of `time.Duration`, and none of its methods
choices.why: Right: `type Span has no field or method Hours`. Converting back to `time.Duration` gets them.

choices.text: `Span` was declared without methods of its own, so it may not call any
choices.why: `Span` has `Days`, and the call to `Hours` is still refused, because `Hours` belongs to `time.Duration`.

prompt: `Weekday` has a `String` method returning the day's name. What does `fmt.Printf("%d", Saturday)` print?
hint: Which verbs did the method change?

choices.text: `Saturday`, since `fmt` calls `String` for every verb
choices.why: It does for `Println`, `%v` and `%s`. `%d` asks for the number.

choices.text: `%!d(main.Weekday=Saturday)`, a wrong-verb complaint
choices.why: `%d` suits a `Weekday`, whose underlying type is `int`, so there is nothing to complain about.
Right. The constant is still the number 6; the method only changes how `%v` and `%s` show it.

choices.text: Nothing: the program panics
choices.why: The output line was `Saturday Saturday 6`, with no panic.

prompt: In `package main`, which of these may be given a method? Choose all that apply.
hint: The type must be defined in the same package, and an alias defines nothing.

choices.text: `type Celsius float64`
choices.why: Yes: a defined type of this package, built on a number.

choices.text: `type Names []string`
choices.why: Yes. A defined slice type is a type of this package like any other.

choices.text: `time.Duration`
choices.why: No: it belongs to the `time` package.

choices.text: `type Count = int`
choices.why: No. The alias is `int`, which is predeclared.

prompt: Why is `strings.ToUpper(s)` a function rather than a method you call as `s.ToUpper()`?
hint: Who defines the type `string`?

choices.text: Functions run faster than methods
choices.why: A method call is a function call with the receiver as the first parameter; speed is not the reason.

choices.text: `string` is predeclared, so a method on it is refused in every package
choices.why: Right. By section 02's rule, `strings` has no way to declare `s.ToUpper()`.

choices.text: Methods are only allowed on struct types
choices.why: `Celsius`, a number, had `ToFahrenheit`, and `time.Weekday`, an `int`, has `String`.

choices.text: Go style forbids methods in the standard library
choices.why: The same package has `Builder`, `Reader` and `Replacer`, each with methods.

prompt: Two functions named `Area`, one taking a `Rect` and one a `Circle`, are refused. Two methods named `Area`, one on each type, compile. Why the difference?
hint: Where does a method's name live?

choices.text: Methods are overloaded by receiver type, and functions by nothing
choices.why: Go has no overloading of either. Each `Area` is a different method because it belongs to a different type.

choices.text: The two methods were in different files
choices.why: They were in the same file, `main.go`; files of one package share a scope anyway.

choices.text: A method's name belongs to its type, and a function's to the package
choices.why: Right: `Area redeclared in this block` for the functions, nothing for the methods.

choices.text: The compiler renames methods to `RectArea` and `CircleArea` itself
choices.why: No renaming happens; `%T` of `Rect.Area` printed `func(main.Rect) float64`, a method of `Rect`.

prompt: Instead of a `String` method, `Weekday` gets `func WeekdayName(d Weekday) string` in the same package. What does `fmt.Println(Saturday)` print?
hint: What does `fmt` look for?

choices.text: `Saturday`: `fmt` finds a function that takes a `Weekday`
choices.why: `fmt` cannot see your package's functions. It looks for a method named `String` on the value's type.
Right. A function nobody calls changes nothing, and lesson 6 printed the same `0 1 6` without one.

choices.text: A compile error, as `Weekday` has no `String`
choices.why: Nothing requires a `String` method; without one `fmt` prints the number.

choices.text: `main.Weekday(6)`, the type and the number
choices.why: `Println` adds no type name to a number; it printed `0 1 6` in lesson 6.

prompt: A package defines `type Money int64`, in cents. It needs `fmt` to print a `Money` as `R$ 19,90`, and it needs the total of a `[]Money`. Which design fits section 03?
hint: One of the two has to be found by `fmt`; the other is about many values.

choices.text: Both functions, `Format(m Money)` and `Total(items []Money)`, as `strings` does
choices.why: `fmt` never calls `Format`; `fmt.Println(price)` would print the number of cents.

choices.text: A `String` method on `Money`, and `Total` as a function taking `[]Money`
choices.why: Right. `fmt` has to find `String` on the type; a total is about many values, with none of them in charge.

choices.text: Both methods on `Money`, with `Total` called on the first item as `items[0].Total(items)`
choices.why: It compiles, and the receiver plays no part in it, which is the sign a function was wanted.

choices.text: A method `String` on `int64`, so every amount prints as money
choices.why: `int64` is not your type: `cannot define new methods on non-local type int64`.

prompt: For which of these is a plain function the natural choice? Choose all that apply.
hint: A method needs one value of a type you own in charge.

choices.text: Counting the vowels in a `string`
choices.why: Yes: `string` cannot have your methods, as `strings` shows.

choices.text: Deciding whether two `Rect` values overlap
choices.why: Yes. Both rectangles play the same part, and `Overlap(a, b)` says so.

choices.text: Making `fmt.Println` show a `Celsius` as `21.5C`
choices.why: No: `fmt` finds a `String` method and nothing else.

choices.text: Computing a `Rect`'s area from its own two fields
choices.why: No. That is one value's own data, the first reason for a method.

prompt: `r` is a `Rect`. What is the type of `r.Area`, written without brackets?
hint: The receiver is already inside it.

choices.text: `float64`, the area
choices.why: Without the brackets nothing is called. The value is the method itself, with `r` filled in.

choices.text: `func(main.Rect) float64`
choices.why: That is `Rect.Area`, the method expression, which still needs a `Rect` as its parameter.

choices.text: `func() float64`
choices.why: Right: a method value, a function with the receiver bound, as `%T` printed.

choices.text: A compile error: a method must be called
choices.why: `area := r.Area` compiled and ran, and `area()` printed 12.

prompt: `r := Rect{W: 3, H: 4}`, then `area := r.Area`, then `r.H = 5`. What does `area()` return?
hint: When was the receiver copied?

prompt: Using section 04's `Shift`, what does `strings.Map(Shift(1).Rotate, "abc z")` return?
hint: `Rotate` wraps from `z` back to `a` and leaves non-letters alone.

choices.text: `abc z`, since a method value cannot carry its 1
choices.why: It does: `Shift(13).Rotate` carried its 13 and turned `hello` into `uryyb`.

choices.text: `bcd!a`
choices.why: The space is not a lower-case letter, so `Rotate` returns it unchanged.

choices.text: `bcd {`
choices.why: `{` comes after `z` in ASCII, and `% 26` is there to wrap back to `a` instead.

choices.text: `bcd a`
choices.why: Right. Each letter moves one place, `z` wraps to `a`, and the space stays.

prompt: `Employee` declares its own `Greet`, yet `e.Introduce()` printed `Hello, I am Ana.` without `from Acme`. Why?
hint: What is the receiver of the promoted `Introduce`?

choices.text: Go always prefers the method of the deeper, embedded type
choices.why: The shallower wins: `e.Greet()` found `Employee`'s. The question is what `Introduce` calls inside.

choices.text: `Introduce` runs on `e.Person`, so its `p.Greet()` is `Person`'s
choices.why: Right. A promoted method receives the embedded value and cannot know an `Employee` is around it.

choices.text: `Employee.Greet` has a different signature, so it does not override
choices.why: Both are `Greet() string`. Nothing in Go overrides, whatever the signature.

choices.text: `Person`'s methods were compiled before `Employee` existed
choices.why: Declaration order does not matter in a package; what matters is that `p` is a `Person`.

prompt: `r` is a `Rect` with a method `Area() float64`. Match each spelling to what it is.
hint: Two of them call, two of them do not.

pairs.right: a method value of type `func() float64`
a method expression of type `func(main.Rect) float64`
the same call as `r.Area()`, with the receiver as first argument

right_distractors: a method promoted from an embedded `Rect`

prompt: Put the pieces of `Rect`'s `Area` method in the order they are written.
hint: The receiver comes before the name.

prompt: `Contractor` embeds `Person`. You add `func (c Contractor) Greet() string` returning `"Hi from " + c.Agency`. What does `c.Introduce()` print now for Caio?
hint: Who is the receiver of `Introduce`?

choices.text: `Hi from Temps.`
choices.why: That would need `Introduce` to call `Contractor`'s `Greet`, and its receiver is the embedded `Person`.

choices.text: `Hello, I am Caio.`
choices.why: Right. Adding a `Greet` to the outer type changes `c.Greet()` and leaves the promoted `Introduce` exactly as it was.

choices.text: A compile error: `Greet` is ambiguous
choices.why: Ambiguity needs two of the same name at the same depth; here one is at depth 0 and wins.

choices.text: `Hi from Temps`, followed by `Hello, I am Caio.`
choices.why: Nothing calls both. `Introduce` makes one call, to `p.Greet()`, on a `Person`.

prompt: A package `geo` defines `Point`. In `package main` you want a type with a `Distance` method that still has `Point`'s own methods. Which declaration gives you that?
hint: Combine section 02's rule with lesson 16.

choices.text: `func (p geo.Point) Distance(q geo.Point) float64`
choices.why: `geo.Point` is not defined in `main`: `cannot define new methods on non-local type`.

choices.text: `type Place = geo.Point` and a method on `Place`
choices.why: An alias is `geo.Point` itself, refused for the same reason as `Number = int`.

choices.text: `type Place struct{ geo.Point }` and a method on `Place`
choices.why: Right. `Place` is defined in `main`, so it may have methods, and `Point`'s own are promoted to it.

choices.text: `type Place geo.Point`, which keeps every method of `Point` and adds `Distance`
choices.why: It compiles, but keeps none of `Point`'s methods, as `Span` lost `Hours`, so it is not what was asked.

prompt: In `~/methods-embed`, how many different methods can be called as `e.X()` on an `Employee`, counting promoted ones but not `e.Person.X()`?
hint: `Person`'s `Greet` is hidden behind `Employee`'s.
